title: Nayeli
text:
I’m an entry level environmental and sustainability professional with field and lab experience in data collection, GIS mapping, and vegetation monitoring. I’ve contributed data to a peer-reviewed publication on invasive species detection.
I’m completing my Professional Science Master’s in Ecosystem Science and Sustainability at Colorado State University, working toward a career in sustainability, with the end goal of Carbon or ESG analyst. I’m interested in water and carbon, with special focus in habitat restoration and wetlands.
Outside of coursework, I volunteer with the Watershed Enhancement Team, led by our tireless leader, Tiffany Swiderski. The team’s work includes invasive species removal, fire mitigation, and watershed clean-ups.

title: Beetle Outbreaks in Grand County, 1997-2025
text:
The question
How has bark beetle damage in Grand County changed over time? Which beetles were responsible, when did each one peak, and has there been any resurgence?

title: Beetle Outbreaks in Grand County, 1997-2025
text:
The Data
I used the aerial detection surveys from the USDA Forest Service, Forest health Protection (Region 2). Each year, surveyors fly over the forest and map the area. I clipped the damage polygons to the Grand County boundary (TIGER) in QGIS, then summed the acres by years and beetle type in R. The beetles were narrowed to the most damaging: mountain pine beetle, spruce beetle, and western balsam bark beetle.

title: Beetle Outbreaks in Grand County, 1997-2025
text:
Beetle Damage Across the Years
Bark beetle damage in Grand County came in waves. Mountain pine beetle damage grew from about 3,187 acres in 1997 to a peak of about 288,000 acres in 2006. Spruce beetle took over 2011 and affected about 15,000 to 19,000 acres a year from 2013 through 2016. By 2025, the mapped damage dropped to about 335 acres total.

title: Beetle Outbreaks in Grand County, 1997-2025
text:
What I found






Damage came in waves. It started small in 1997 with about 3,200 acres, and the mountain pine beetle spread, peaking in 2006 at about 288,000 acres in a single year. From 2011 onward, the spruce beetle took over, but at a smaller scale: about 15,000 to 19,000 acres a year from 2013 to 2016. Spruce beetle had one rebound in 2018, at about 16,600 acres, but mostly declined. Current data would suggest there are low levels of major beetles, with the exception of the western balsam bark beetle which has shown fairly consistent damage.

title: Beetle Outbreaks in Grand County, 1997-2025
text:
Limits
Aerial surveys map damage by eye from the air, so they can show patterns, but are not exact.
Survey conditions can change year to year, so changes may reflect on the survey, not the beetles.

title: Beetle-Killed Forest and Wildfire Risk, Grand County, Colorado
text:
The Question
Where are residential communities in Grand County exposed to wildfire fuels in beetle-killed forest, and which communities should a vulnerability assessment focus on?

title: Beetle-Killed Forest and Wildfire Risk, Grand County, Colorado
text:
Study Area
Grand County covers 1,846 square miles and has about 16,500 residents. About 70% of the land is federally owned. The county’s wildfire protection plan (CWPP) maps 30 communities. I narrowed these to three that sit in different parts of the county, so their hazards differ: Big Horn Park, Southern Grand Lake, and Sunset Ridge.

title: Beetle-Killed Forest and Wildfire Risk, Grand County, Colorado
text:
What I Found
Lodgepole pine covers 17.9% of Southern Grand Lake, 13.6% of Sunset Ridge, and 6.3% of Big Horn Park, using LANDFIRE fuel data. The fuel mixes differ between the communities as a whole.
